questions.q: What is the key difference between Date and Datetime in Apex?
options: Date holds a calendar day with no time; Datetime holds both a day and a time
They are the same type with two different names
Date can only be used in triggers
Datetime cannot be compared with comparison operators
questions.explain: A Date value represents a calendar day with no time component, while a Datetime value represents a specific day and time together.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend `String.isBlank()` over a plain `someString == null` check?
options: isBlank() is simply faster to type, with no functional difference
A null check throws a compile error in Apex, so isBlank() is required
isBlank() catches null, empty string, and whitespace-only strings all in one check, while a plain null check misses the other two cases
isBlank() only works on sObject fields, not plain variables
questions.explain: String.isBlank() returns true for null, '', and whitespace-only strings, while someString == null alone would miss the empty and whitespace-only cases.

An Integer representing the count of commas

questions.explain: String.split() divides a string on the given delimiter and returns a List<String> of the resulting pieces, in order.

options: Throws a compile-time error, since Dates can't be parsed from Strings
Parses a YYYY-MM-DD formatted String into a Date value
Returns the current date, ignoring the input String entirely
Returns a Datetime, not a Date
questions.explain: Date.valueOf() parses a String in YYYY-MM-DD format into a Date, and throws an exception at runtime if the format doesn't match exactly.

questions.q: Can Date values be compared directly with operators like `<` and `>` in Apex?
options: Yes — Date and Datetime values support direct comparison operators such as <, >, and ==
No, Dates must be converted to Integers first using a system method
Only Datetime supports comparison operators, not Date
Only using a special Date.compareTo() method, never operators
questions.explain: Date and Datetime values support the standard comparison operators directly, which is what makes checks like opp.CloseDate < Date.today() work naturally.
